blocks.title: Why we cook
blocks.md: Cooking makes food **safe** (kills many germs), **palatable** (flavour, texture, appearance) and **easier to digest**. Methods using **water**: boiling, simmering, steaming, stewing. Methods using **fat**: frying (shallow and deep). Methods using **dry heat**: roasting, grilling, baking.

blocks.title: Changes on heating
blocks.md: **Starch** grains absorb water and burst (**gelatinisation**), thickening a sauce. **Proteins** **coagulate** (set) as an egg white turns solid; over-cooking makes them tough. **Fats** melt; very high heat makes oil smoke and break down. **Vitamin C** and some B vitamins are lost in cooking, mostly into the water.

blocks.caption: A table grouping cooking methods by water, fat and dry heat.
blocks.alt: Table of cooking methods by medium: water, fat and dry heat.

blocks.title: Keeping nutrients
blocks.md: Wash before cutting; do not soak; cook in a small amount of water for a short time; use the cooking water; do not add bicarbonate of soda (it destroys some vitamins); serve soon after cooking; fry in moderate amounts of fresh oil; avoid burning.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Deep-frying adds a lot of energy from fat.
- Never leave hot oil unattended: fat fires need a lid, not water.
- Cassava products must be prepared properly (peeling, soaking, fermenting, drying and cooking as traditionally done) to be safe. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why does a sauce thicken when flour or cornflour is heated in it?
steps: Starch grains absorb water and swell.
They burst and the starch forms a thick gel (gelatinisation).

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose a method for each aim: (a) low fat, (b) crisp texture, (c) soft tender meat cooked slowly.
steps: (a) Steaming or grilling adds little fat. (b) Frying or roasting gives crispness.

blocks.title: Contamination and food poisoning
blocks.md: Food can be contaminated by **bacteria**, **viruses**, **moulds**, chemicals or physical objects. Sources: hands, raw meat and fish, flies and pests, dirty water, unwashed utensils, soil. **Food poisoning** may cause vomiting, diarrhoea and fever. Young children, the elderly and sick people are at greater risk.

blocks.title: Bacteria and temperature
blocks.md: Bacteria multiply fastest in warm, moist, protein-rich foods, roughly between 5 °C and 60 °C (the 'danger zone', flagged for review). They may double in number about every 20 minutes in good conditions (illustration only). Keep cold food cold (fridge below about 5 °C), hot food hot, and cook food until very hot all the way through (about 70 °C or more in the centre).

blocks.caption: A bar chart showing bacteria doubling every 20 minutes from 1 to 16 in 80 minutes.
blocks.alt: Bar chart: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 bacteria at 0, 20, 40, 60 and 80 minutes, an illustration of doubling.

blocks.title: Hygiene rules
blocks.md: **Personal**: wash hands with soap, clean clothes or apron, tie hair back, cover cuts, do not cough over food. **Food**: buy fresh food, wash fruit and vegetables, separate raw and cooked, cover food, cool and store leftovers promptly. **Kitchen**: clean surfaces, wash cloths, dispose of waste, control flies and rats, safe water.

blocks.title: Kitchen safety
blocks.md: Prevent burns (handles in, careful with hot oil), cuts (sharp knives used properly), electric shocks (dry hands, no damaged wires), slips (wipe spills), gas hazards (check cylinders and connections). Keep a first-aid kit and know basic first aid; learn from a trained person.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Food may look and smell normal and still be unsafe.
- Leftovers should not be reheated many times.
- Temperature values here are general; local food safety authorities give exact limits. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Growth
blocks.statement: One bacterium doubles every 20 minutes in warm food (illustration). How many are there after 2 hours?

blocks.title: Example 2 - Spot the faults
blocks.statement: A cook handles raw fish, wipes hands on her apron and chops salad on the same board. List the faults.
steps: She did not wash her hands with soap after raw fish.

blocks.title: Spoilage
blocks.md: **Spoilage** is the process that makes food unfit to eat. Causes: **microorganisms** (bacteria, yeasts and moulds) and **enzymes** in the food itself (for example ripening and browning). Signs: bad smell, slime, mould, change of colour and taste, swelling of cans.

blocks.title: Conditions for growth
blocks.md: Microorganisms need **food**, **moisture**, **warmth**, **suitable pH** and (for many) **oxygen**, and time. Preservation works by removing, reducing or blocking one or more of these, or by killing the microorganisms.

blocks.caption: A table of four preservation methods with the principle behind each.
blocks.alt: Table: drying removes water, refrigeration uses cold, canning uses heat and sealing, salting draws out water.

blocks.title: Methods
blocks.md: **Drying/smoking** (dried fish, crayfish, smoked meat): removes water. **Salting and sugar**: draw out water. **Refrigeration** (about 0-5 °C) slows growth; **freezing** (about -18 °C) stops growth, but does not kill all germs. **Canning**: heat in sealed cans. **Pickling**: acid (vinegar). **Fermentation**: useful microorganisms make acid (e.g. yoghurt, fermented cassava products).

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Freezing does not kill all bacteria; they can grow again after thawing.
- Do not refreeze thawed food.
- Moulds on groundnuts and maize can produce toxins (aflatoxins); dry well and store properly; discard mouldy or shrivelled nuts.
- Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1 - Principle
blocks.statement: Explain why smoked and dried fish keeps for longer than fresh fish.
steps: Drying and smoking remove most of the water, so growth is stopped.

blocks.title: Example 2 - Choose
blocks.statement: A farmer in Bamenda has a large harvest of groundnuts. How can he store them safely?
steps: Dry them well in the sun on a clean surface.
Store in clean, dry, ventilated containers off the ground; check for mould and discard bad nuts.
